chunks: Multiphase impact on efficiency. The question: How do they impact efficiency?
Whether multiphase is more efficient depends on which loss you look at. Conduction loss, the I to the 2R heat, drops when the current is split among phases.
Fixed losses, such as gate drive, grow with every active phase. So multiphase tends to help at heavy load and hurt at light load. Phase shedding fixes the light-load problem.
Imagine carrying 60 kg. One person struggles, and the strain grows faster than the weight. Four people each carrying 15 kg strain far less each, and in total much less.
That is the I squared effect. But four people need four lunches whether or not the load is heavy. Those lunches are the fixed losses.
The analogy has a catch: one person four times as strong (one big stage with four times the switch size) would strain no more than the team, and the example shows this.
The dashed curves are 1, 2 and 4 active phases with the same per-phase power stage (the model of the table above).
The red curve is the envelope you get by choosing the phase count at each load: that is phase shedding.
Notice the crossovers: 4 phases beat 2 above roughly 17 amps in this model, and a single phase beats 2 below roughly 8. 5 amps.
Conduction loss: heat from current through resistance, I to the 2R ("Why buck beats LDO efficiency").
Fixed losses: power each phase spends just running (driving its switches, its inductor core, its controller), which does not shrink with load.
Phase shedding: switching off phases at light load. Switching loss: energy lost at each turn-on and turn-off.
Phase count ( N ): how many phases are in parallel ("What a multiphase buck is").
Give each phase FETs and an inductor totaling 4 milliohms. Four phases at 15 amps each lose 4 times 15 squared times 0. 004 equals 3. 6 watts.
One stage with the same 4 milliohms at 60 amps would lose 60 squared times 0. 004 equals 14. 4 watts.
But a single stage built with four times as much switch area (silicon), 1 milliohms, loses 60 squared times 0. 001 equals 3. 6 watts, the same. That is the whole idea.
"Multiphase efficiency depends on the loss. Conduction loss is I to the 2R : with the same per-phase parts it falls as 1 over N, but for the same total silicon it is unchanged.
Switching loss in total is about the same.
Gate drive, driver quiescent and core loss grow with the number of phases, so at light load a multiphase buck is less efficient unless it sheds phases.
So it's better at high load and needs phase shedding to stay efficient at low load."
